parental occupational exposures were not associated with an increased risk for childhood cancer, with the exception of a small risk for leukaemia associated with paternal periconception exposure to exhaust fume, driving, and inhaled particulate.
parental occupation at periconceptual period is not associated with an increased risk for childhood cancer.
parental occupation at conception does not increase the risk of childhood cancers, with the possible exception of a small increase in risk for vehicle related exposure.

the effects of parental occupational exposures on the risk of childhood cancers.
the possible effects of environmental and occupational exposures on human health, and in particular on the risk of developing childhood cancer.
the possible role of parental occupational exposures to environmental agents in the aetiology of childhood cancers.

the evidence for an association between parental occupation and childhood cancer is limited and inconclusive.
no strong evidence has been found linking occupational exposures of parents with an increased risk in childhood cancer.

the findings do not support the hypothesis of an increased risk of leukaemia and other cancers associated with paternal exposure to ionising radiations, although the numbers are limited.
